prompt: Household incomes in a county are strongly right-skewed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. A researcher takes a random sample of $n = 50$ households. Which statement about the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{x}$ is correct?

choices.label: It is strongly right-skewed, like the population.
It is approximately normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{50}$.
It is approximately normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.
Its mean is less than $\mu$ because the sample pulls toward the typical household.

hint: Two separate facts: the CLT handles the SHAPE, and $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ handles the SPREAD.

hints.text: Two separate facts: the CLT handles the SHAPE, and $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ handles the SPREAD.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: from ANY population, $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$ and $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$ — that rules out two choices right away. Then ask what the CLT says about shape when $n = 50$.
A sample of 50 is large enough ($n \ge 30$) for the CLT to make $\bar{x}$ approximately normal even from a skewed population. The SD must have $\sqrt{n}$ in it.
B: approximately normal, centered at $\mu$, with SD $\sigma/\sqrt{50}$.

explanation: Center: $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$ always, so D is wrong — sample means are unbiased.
Shape: the population is skewed, but $n = 50 \ge 30$, so by the Central Limit Theorem $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal. A is wrong; B is correct.

alternativeExplanations.title: What if n were small?
steps: With $n = 3$, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ would still be noticeably right-skewed — the CLT needs a decent sample size.
Even then, its mean would be $\mu$ and its SD would be $\sigma/\sqrt{3}$.
At $n = 50$ the skew has mostly averaged out, giving choice B.
